Dermatology · published research

Eyebrow loss

In one uncontrolled study of 16 women with frontal fibrosing alopecia, eyebrow-hair counts increased after ten weekly LED sessions and remained higher than baseline at six months. The change is encouraging but cannot be separated from natural variation or other treatment effects because no comparison group was included.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

One single-arm study in women with frontal fibrosing alopecia found higher eyebrow-hair counts after LED treatment and at six-month follow-up. Because the study had no untreated or sham group, it cannot determine how much of the change was caused by the light treatment.

Summary of the Evidence

In 16 women with eyebrow loss associated with frontal fibrosing alopecia, eyebrow-hair counts increased after ten weekly sessions and remained above baseline six months later. This is an objective but uncontrolled result from one small cohort, so the size of any treatment effect remains uncertain.

Human and clinical evidence

Gerkowicz et al. treated 16 women aged 60–74 with red LED light once weekly for ten weeks. The median total eyebrow-hair count was 132 before treatment, 152 after the tenth session, and 176 at the six-month follow-up. Both post-treatment and follow-up counts were higher than baseline (p = 0.002). The study reported good tolerability. It had no sham or untreated comparison, and its findings apply to eyebrow loss in frontal fibrosing alopecia rather than other causes of thinning (Gerkowicz et al. 2021).

Animal evidence

No animal evidence was identified for PBM treatment of eyebrow loss.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The study used a 630 ± 5 nm red LED array at 37 J/cm² and 68 mW/cm². Each session lasted about nine minutes and four seconds, with treatment once weekly for ten weeks. The eyebrows and frontal hairline were irradiated. The paper identifies the device as the Red Beam pro+, Model APRO. This single protocol does not establish whether another dose or schedule would produce a similar result (Gerkowicz et al. 2021).

Interpretation

Eyebrow-hair counts were higher after treatment and remained above baseline at six months in this cohort. The absence of a comparison group means natural fluctuation, concurrent care, and measurement conditions cannot be ruled out. Controlled replication in people with frontal fibrosing alopecia is needed to estimate the treatment effect.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

In 16 women, the median total eyebrow-hair count rose from 132 at baseline to 152 after ten sessions and 176 at six months. Counts at both later assessments were higher than baseline (p = 0.002); the study had no untreated or sham group (Gerkowicz et al. 2021).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for eyebrow-hair-count change in frontal fibrosing alopecia. The result comes from one 16-person, single-arm study without a comparator, although counts were assessed again six months after treatment.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The study used objective trichoscopic counts at baseline, after ten sessions, and six months later, which documents change over time. However, no sham or untreated group was included, and only one cohort has been reported. Natural fluctuation, concurrent management, and measurement conditions therefore remain possible explanations for some of the change (Gerkowicz et al. 2021).
